goal: By the end you can look at a signal in time or frequency, explain how rotating vectors and orthogonal sinusoids reveal its ingredients, and predict what convolution filters will do.

lessons.objective: By the end you can describe how a chain of rotating vectors makes a moving tip trace a shape.

beats.text: Watch a few nested circles move a pen tip into a recognizable heart.
How can simple circular motions cooperate to make corners, lobes, and a pointed bottom?
Follow the endpoint of one rotor, then attach a second rotor to that endpoint and add their displacements.
The final pen position is a sum of rotating vectors; each circle contributes one rhythm and one scale.
The same idea can describe a drawing, a vibration, or any signal built from repeated motion.
One rotor gives a circle; many rotors add their tips to trace richer paths.

visuals.title: Every sound is a sum of circles
visuals.goal: Make the moving endpoint and its nested circular scaffolding obvious, then show that summed rotors rebuild waves, a square wave, and a drawing.

visuals.title: Let the rotors draw a shape
visuals.goal: Let the learner vary the number and speed of rotating components.

lessons.objective: By the end you can use the complex plane to interpret multiplication by a unit complex number as a rotation.

beats.text: Press the button i and watch an arrow turn exactly a quarter-turn without changing length.
What arithmetic operation could carry both the size and direction of a planar arrow?
Place a+bi at the point (a,b), then multiply polar lengths and add polar angles.
Multiplying by cos(θ)+i sin(θ) rotates by θ; its magnitude is one, so no stretch occurs.
Complex numbers let a two-dimensional rotation become one compact multiplication rule.
A complex number is a plane point, and complex multiplication composes scale and turn.

visuals.title: The complex plane turns
visuals.goal: Connect a+bi, polar angle, and rotation by multiplication.

lessons.objective: By the end you can read e^{iωt} as a unit vector with angular speed ω and identify how a coefficient changes its size and phase.

beats.text: Compare two clock hands: one turns twice as fast, while another starts from a different angle.
Which part of a compact formula should control speed, length, and starting angle?
Track e^{iωt} around the unit circle and multiply it by a fixed complex coefficient.
ω sets angular speed, the coefficient magnitude sets radius, and its angle sets phase.
A signal can be assembled by adding many independent clock hands with different speeds.
Complex exponentials are rotating basis motions, with coefficients carrying amplitude and phase.

visuals.title: A complex clock hand
visuals.goal: Separate angular speed, amplitude, and phase in one rotating vector.

lessons.objective: By the end you can derive a sine wave as the one-axis projection of uniform circular motion.

beats.text: A bead loops around a circle while its shadow slides up and down as a perfect wave.
Why does a constant-speed circle produce a changing signal with smooth peaks and troughs?
Project the rotor's endpoint onto the vertical axis and label the height at equal time steps.
The projected coordinate is A sin(ωt+φ), so amplitude, frequency, and phase have geometric jobs.
Every pure sinusoid is a simple rotating ingredient viewed through one coordinate.
Rotation in the plane and oscillation on a line are two views of the same motion.

visuals.title: A sine wave is a shadow
visuals.goal: Make projection from a rotating vector to a sinusoid visually immediate.

lessons.objective: By the end you can distinguish frequency, period, angular frequency, and amplitude when comparing oscillations.

beats.text: Two equal-height waves race across the screen: one completes six cycles while the other completes two.
What changed between the waves, and what stayed fixed?
Measure one cycle as a period T, count cycles per time as f, and convert to angular speed ω=2πf.
Frequency changes the horizontal spacing and tempo; amplitude changes vertical reach.
The spectrum will use frequency as its address, so a clear sense of pace matters more than a memorized symbol.
Period is time per cycle, frequency is cycles per time, and angular frequency counts radians per time.

visuals.title: Tempo versus height
visuals.goal: Separate frequency from amplitude and period with matched wave comparisons.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why averaging a signal times a reference sinusoid detects the reference frequency.

beats.text: A detector listens to a messy signal and lights up only when its reference rhythm matches a hidden tone.
How can multiplication and averaging tell one frequency apart from all the others?
Multiply the signal by a reference sine, inspect the positive and negative lobes, and average over complete cycles.
Matching rhythms stay biased in one sign and produce a nonzero inner product; mismatched rhythms cancel.
This is a projection onto a sinusoidal direction, just like a dot product finds a vector's component.
Tune the reference, multiply, and average: the result measures that sinusoid's coefficient.

visuals.title: Tune the rhythm detector
visuals.goal: Show matching products accumulating while mismatches cancel.

lessons.objective: By the end you can use sinusoidal orthogonality to justify measuring Fourier coefficients independently.

beats.text: Multiply two different integer-frequency waves and watch their product paint equal positive and negative area.
When does one rhythm become invisible to another under an inner product?
Integrate over a shared complete period and pair sine with sine, cosine with cosine, and sine with cosine.
Distinct harmonics have zero inner product, while a wave paired with itself has positive energy.
Sinusoids act like perpendicular coordinate axes in a space of functions.
Orthogonality is the cancellation rule that lets each frequency be read without contamination from the others.

visuals.title: Rhythms as perpendicular axes
visuals.goal: Make zero cross-correlation and positive self-correlation visible.

lessons.objective: By the end you can describe a periodic signal as a constant plus weighted sine and cosine harmonics.

beats.text: A single sine wave grows extra harmonics until its smooth crest becomes a square wave's flat top.
Can a repeating shape be rebuilt from a vocabulary of pure tones?
Project the periodic signal onto each orthogonal sine and cosine, then add the measured coefficients.
The Fourier series is the sum of harmonics; more terms add sharper detail while preserving the periodic pattern.
The drawing made by rotating vectors and the sound made by harmonics use the same additive language.
Fourier series = constant term plus orthogonal sinusoidal ingredients, each weighted by projection.

visuals.title: Build a periodic shape from tones
visuals.goal: Show harmonics accumulating into a repeating waveform.

visuals.title: Watch circles build a heart
visuals.goal: Connect sorted Fourier coefficients to a reconstruction that sharpens as terms are added.

lessons.objective: By the end you can interpret the continuous Fourier transform as a correlation with every possible frequency.

beats.text: A frequency spotlight sweeps across a one-time pulse and paints a broad spectrum instead of a few discrete bars.
What changes when the signal is not periodic and the candidate frequencies are no longer integer harmonics?
Correlate the signal with e^{-iωt} for each real ω, recording magnitude and phase as the detector scans.
The transform turns time localization into a spread of frequencies and turns repeated rhythms into concentrated peaks.
Time and frequency are complementary descriptions, connected by a reversible integral transform with a convention-dependent scale.
The Fourier transform is a continuum of rhythm detectors, not a mysterious switch that deletes the signal's structure.

visuals.title: Scan every frequency
visuals.goal: Connect a time signal to its continuous magnitude and phase spectrum.

lessons.objective: By the end you can predict how a time-domain convolution changes a signal by inspecting the filter's frequency response.

beats.text: A sliding blur kernel softens a jagged signal while a frequency mask dims its fast rotors.
Why should sliding weighted overlap in time be equivalent to multiplying spectra?
Write convolution as accumulated shifted copies of a kernel, then transform the shifts into phase factors.
The convolution theorem turns convolution into pointwise multiplication: each frequency is scaled and phase-shifted independently.
Low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass filters are choices about which rotating ingredients survive.
Convolution is overlap in time and multiplication in frequency, so filtering is easiest to see in the spectrum.

visuals.title: Filtering as frequency choice
visuals.goal: Link sliding overlap, spectral multiplication, and selective frequency loss.
